title: Hesse Eigenvalues: Curvature Along the Principal Axes
topic: The Hesse matrix is symmetric, so it diagonalises in an orthonormal basis: its eigenvectors are the principal directions of curvature and its eigenvalues are the curvatures along them. Both eigenvalues positive — local minimum. Both negative — local maximum. Mixed signs — saddle. Connects the second-derivative test back to chapter 4 diagonalisation.

beats.narration: The Hesse matrix is symmetric, so it has a hidden pair of perpendicular axes. Those are where the curvature really lives.

elements.content: Manimo bobs centre, caption 'Two axes of curvature.'

beats.narration: Take a tilted bowl. Its contours are tilted ellipses. Find the two perpendicular directions whose principal axes match the ellipse. Those are the eigenvectors of the Hesse matrix.

elements.content: Tilted elliptical contours (rotated by 25°) on chalk-300 axes
Eigenvector v₁ along the long principal axis, violet-400, labelled
Eigenvector v₂ along the short principal axis, teal-400, labelled, perpendicular to v₁
Right panel: 'principal axes' eyebrow + 'H v_i = lambda_i v_i' formula + footnote 'the curvature axes that the matrix itself picks out'

beats.narration: Rotate into that frame, and the Hesse matrix becomes diagonal — its two eigenvalues sitting on the diagonal. Those are the curvatures along the principal axes.

elements.content: Big serif formula: H = P D P^T with D = diag(lambda_1, lambda_2), columns of P highlighted violet and teal

beats.narration: The signs of the eigenvalues classify the point. Both positive — bowl. Both negative — dome. One of each — saddle. The discriminant just tracks the product, lambda one times lambda two.

elements.content: Three small cards side by side: BOTH POSITIVE → MIN (emerald), BOTH NEGATIVE → MAX (rose), MIXED SIGNS → SADDLE (amber). Each card shows two stacked eigenvalue badges and a tiny verdict line.
Bottom caption 'sign of det H = sign of lambda_1 lambda_2 = D'

beats.narration: Same algebra as chapter four — diagonalise the matrix and let its eigenvalues do the talking.
